chapter: Tip 1 — Care About Your Craft
idea: Care about the craft: software quality is a personal professional choice, not an organizational mandate.
application: In briefs and reviews, treat quality bars (tests, clarity, small PRs) as the user's own standards, not someone else's imposition.

chapter: Tip 2 — Think! About Your Work
idea: Work deliberately: understand what you're doing while you do it — active thought beats rote process.
application: Before suggesting a plan, ask what the user is really trying to change; a suggestion without an understood goal is noise.

chapter: Tip 3 — Provide Options, Don't Make Lame Excuses
idea: Own problems and bring options: state what you can do next, not who or what is to blame.
application: When a capture or triage blocks the user, always frame next steps as concrete options ('you can ship partial, postpone, or ask X') instead of dead ends.

chapter: Tip 4 — Don't Live with Broken Windows
idea: Leave no small defects unfixed: broken windows signal abandonment and accelerate decay.
application: Small visible bugs deserve a scheduled fix task (not_urgent_important) rather than being dropped; escalate silently rotting systems.

chapter: Tip 5 — Be a Catalyst for Change
idea: Be a catalyst: construct a small win, show results before asking for approval to improve everything.
application: For improvement goals, propose the smallest demonstrable slice first; show progress early instead of lobbying for big plans.

chapter: Tip 7 — Make Quality a Requirements Issue
idea: Define acceptable quality explicitly: quality is negotiable per requirement, and 'near enough' can be deliberate.
application: Match effort to the requirement — prototype-grade for experiments, production-grade only where stakes demand it.

chapter: Tip 8 — Invest Regularly in Your Knowledge Portfolio
idea: Diversify and grow your knowledge portfolio: learn several languages, one every few years, a little bit regularly.
application: Feed the daily learning loop: standing 30-minute learning tasks (books, feed articles, LeetCode) are long-block schedule-class work that compounds.

chapter: Tip 9 — Critically Analyze What You Read and Hear
idea: Critically analyze what you read: take vendor claims, blog posts, and AI output as starting points requiring verification.
application: When briefing or capture draws on feed articles or LLM suggestions, surface the source and invite verification before committing to action.

chapter: Tip 10 — It's Both What You Say and the Way You Say It
idea: Communication is the deliverable too: respect the audience's knowledge, agenda, and vocabulary; plan what you want to say.
application: Draft summaries and briefs for the reader's context first — what do they need to decide — not what we did next.

chapter: Tip 11 — DRY—Don't Repeat Yourself
idea: Every piece of knowledge must have one authoritative representation; duplication is the smallest lie that grows into sync bugs.
application: Generated work items must not duplicate tracked tasks — reuse the existing task, link it, or deduplicate before proposing work.

chapter: Tip 13 — Eliminate Effects Between Unrelated Things
idea: Design components self-contained with well-defined interfaces so unrelated things stay unrelated (orthogonality).
application: When scoping work, split tightly-coupled efforts into orthogonal tasks so one delay doesn't block unrelated goals.

chapter: Tip 14 — There Are No Final Decisions
idea: Treat every decision as provisional: build reversible decisions, and revisit irreversible ones deliberately.
application: When the user locks a plan, ask two things: what would prove this wrong, and what's the cheapest way to stay revisable.

chapter: Tip 15 — Use Tracer Bullets to Find the Target
idea: Build a thin tracer bullet end-to-end to align on requirements early — a skeleton that runs beats a spec that hopes.
application: Turn airy goals ('build X') into a first full-stack slice task with a date, so reality gets to correct the plan early.

chapter: Tip 16 — Prototype to Learn
idea: Prototype to answer a specific risk, and throw the prototype away — its value is the learning, not the code.
application: Spike tasks must say what question they answer and default to disposable; never let a spike quietly become production.

chapter: Tip 18 — Estimate to Avoid Surprises
idea: Estimate by the magnitude of the range you need, learn from estimate-vs-actual deltas, and distribute estimates across tasks.
application: Bigger tasks get split until a task's size is predictable; plans must carve explicit validation time to check estimates.

chapter: Tip 19 — Iterate the Schedule with the Code
idea: Re-estimate as work progresses: refining the schedule against reality beats finishing a fantasy schedule.
application: Mid-week, re-baseline carried-over tasks — the weekly review should treat repeated slippage as a signal to cut scope, not pad needs.

chapter: Tip 24 — Fix the Problem, Not the Blame
idea: When something breaks, diagnose the system, not the person; blame blocks the information you need.
application: In triage and reviews, phrase failures systemically ('what allowed this to slip') and schedule the diagnostic task over the accusation.

chapter: Tip 25 — Don't Panic
idea: In incidents, breathe first: panic causes wrong tools, fixated causes, and shallow 'fixes'.
application: Urgent_important captures should carry verification steps (reproduce, isolate) rather than instant spray actions.

chapter: Tip 27 — Don't Assume It—Prove It
idea: Debug by proving hypotheses with real data, not by assuming the bug is elsewhere or people's reports are wrong.
application: Before scheduling 'fix' work, task a reproduce/verify step; assumptions in the report should be checked, not carried.

chapter: Tip 32 — Crash Early
idea: Fail fast, fail loudly: dead programs kill less harm than crippled ones that corrupt data.
application: For pipeline-ish tasks (connectors, webhooks), include an early failure check as first acceptance criterion.

chapter: Tip 35 — Finish What You Start
idea: Deallocate responsibly: leave nothing dangling — dot every i, close every resource, complete every handoff.
application: Carried-over tasks risk being 'started' twice; prefer closing (done/archived) explicitly over indefinite drift.

chapter: Tip 37 — Configure, Don't Integrate
idea: Put behavior outside the codebase: configuration makes platforms change without recompiles.
application: Recurring workflows (good candidates for capture→task) should be parameterizable, not hard-coded habits.

chapter: Tip 38 — Put Abstractions in Code, Details in Metadata
idea: Keep decisions changeable: details live in data/metadata so policy shifts don't require code archaeology.
application: For task suggestions, structure meta-driven fields (source links, ids) so future automation can rework them without resets.

chapter: Tip 51 — Iterate: Some Things Can't Be Determined Up Front
idea: Some work cannot be fully planned; iterate until learning replaces the guess.
application: When a requirement is genuinely unknown, propose a learning-first task (research, prototype) instead of a full-build guess.

chapter: Tip 55 — Don't Outthink Your Tools
idea: Know your tooling's limits and trust its well-proven strengths; fighting the toolset wastes the leverage it provides.
application: Prefer standard practices the stack knows (lint, tests, migrations) over clever bespoke machinery the user must maintain alone.

chapter: Tip 58 — Don't Repeat Yourself in Documentation Either
idea: Documentation is a system part of the deliverable — keep it lean, principled, and driven from real sources.
application: Notes captured as tasks keep original references (URLs, ticket ids) in meta so context survives handoffs.

chapter: Tip 60 — Test Early, Test Often, Test Automatically
idea: Untested code cannot be trusted to work; automated tests are the only way to keep craft honest as systems grow.
application: Anything ship-grade suggested should name its test plan; 'add tests' is a legitimate not_urgent_important follow-on task.
